pred_answer: No. Inferring employees' emotions from webcam feeds in the workplace is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(f), which bans placing on the market, putting into service, or using AI systems to infer emotions of natural persons in the areas of workplace and education institutions. The only carve-out is where the system is put in place for medical or safety reasons, such as fatigue detection for accident prevention, and flagging disengagement for management purposes is neither. The system meets the Article 3(39) definition of an emotion recognition system, since it infers emotions from biometric data, namely facial images captured by webcam. Because the prohibition applies, the deployer cannot cure it through the Annex III.1(c) high-risk route or the Article 50(3) duty to inform exposed natural persons; those apply only to emotion recognition permitted outside the workplace and education settings.

Article 5(1)(g). The system is a biometric categorisation system within Article 3(40), and Article 5(1)(g) prohibits placing on the market, putting into service for this specific purpose, or use of biometric categorisation systems that categorise individually natural persons based on their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Facial images are biometric data under Article 3(34), and inferring race, political opinions and sexual orientation falls squarely within that closed list of sensitive attributes. The only carve-out is the labelling or filtering of lawfully acquired biometric datasets, or categorising of biometric data in the area of law enforcement, which does not cover deducing sensitive attributes about individuals.

Yes. Article 5(1)(e) prohibits the placing on the market, the putting into service for this specific purpose, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage. The vendor's indiscriminate harvesting of images from both sources to build such a database falls squarely within that prohibition, which is absolute and carries no carve-out for commercial or security purposes. Because the practice is prohibited, the high-risk analysis under Article 6 and the Annex III biometrics use cases does not arise, and no conformity assessment or transparency measure can cure it. The vendor must cease the scraping and delete the unlawfully constituted database; only targeted collection of facial images on a lawful basis remains available.

Yes. Such an app is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(b), which bans placing on the market, putting into service, or using an AI system that exploits vulnerabilities of a natural person or a specific group due to their age, disability, or a specific social or economic situation, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour in a manner that causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm. Elderly persons with cognitive decline fall squarely within the age and disability vulnerability limbs, and steering them into expensive subscriptions they would not otherwise purchase is material behavioural distortion causing significant financial harm. Where the app also deploys subliminal, purposefully manipulative, or deceptive techniques that appreciably impair the ability to make an informed decision, Article 5(1)(a) is independently breached. No risk management or transparency measure cures a prohibited practice, so the provider must cease placing it on the market and withdraw it; market surveillance authorities may require withdrawal or recall under Article 79 where the system presents a risk to health, safety, or fundamental rights.

Prohibited. Untargeted real-time remote biometric identification of all passers-by in a city square is caught by Article 5.1, point (h), which bans the use of real-time remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes, a city square being a publicly accessible space. Use is lawful only where strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives: the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation, or for missing persons under Article 5.1, point (h)(i); the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or a genuine and present or foreseeable terrorist attack under Article 5.1, point (h)(ii); and the localisation or identification of a suspect of an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years' custody under Article 5.1, point (h)(iii). Blanket scanning of every passer-by meets none of those objectives, and Article 5.2 in any event confines permitted use to temporal, geographic and personal limitations, requires a completed fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27, and Article 5.3 requires prior judicial or administrative authorisation, with Article 5.5 leaving Member States free to authorise those exceptions in national law or impose stricter rules. Where a targeted deployment does fall within an exception, the system remains high-risk under Annex III.1, point (a) as a remote biometric identification system, so the deployer must apply human oversight including the Article 14.5 rule that no action be taken on an identification unless separately verified by at least two competent natural persons, unless national law deems that disproportionate for law enforcement, must use the system per its instructions for use and retain the automatically generated logs for at least six months under Article 26.1 and Article 26.6, and registration occurs in the secure non-public section of the EU database under Article 49.4.

High-risk. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of the supply of electricity falls squarely within Annex III.2 on critical infrastructure, and Article 6.2 classifies any AI system referred to in Annex III as high-risk. The Article 6.3 derogation does not assist here, since managing grid supply is not a narrow procedural task, an improvement of a previously completed human activity, the detection of decision-making patterns, or a preparatory task. The deployer must therefore use the system in accordance with the instructions for use under Article 26.1, assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support under Article 26.2, ensure input data under its control is relevant and sufficiently representative under Article 26.4, monitor operation and report risks and serious incidents under Article 26.5, and retain the automatically generated logs for at least six months under Article 26.6.

The provider must ensure the high-risk AI system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure referred to in Article 43 before it is placed on the market or put into service, as required by Article 16.1.f. That assessment presupposes technical documentation drawn up under Article 11 with the Annex IV content and a quality management system operated under Article 17. Once conformity is demonstrated, the provider draws up the written, machine-readable, signed EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 containing the Annex V information and keeps it at the disposal of national competent authorities for 10 years, then affixes the CE marking under Article 48. For an Annex III system the provider must also register itself and the system in the EU database under Article 49.1 before placing it on the market, and a provider established outside the Union must first appoint an authorised representative by written mandate under Article 22.

Article 15.1 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed so as to achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, and to perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle. Article 15.2 supports this through the development of benchmarks and measurement methodologies for the technical aspects of measuring those levels. The levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics must be declared in the accompanying instructions of use under Article 15.3, and Article 13.3.b.ii requires those instructions to state the accuracy, including its metrics, robustness and cybersecurity against which the system was tested and validated, together with any known and foreseeable circumstances that may affect those expected levels. Article 15.4 requires resilience as regards errors, faults or inconsistencies within the system or the environment in which it operates, addressed where appropriate through technical redundancy solutions such as back-up or fail-safe plans, and requires systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market to be developed so as to eliminate or reduce the risk of biased outputs from feedback loops. Article 15.5 requires resilience against attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter the system's use, outputs or performance by exploiting system vulnerabilities, with technical solutions appropriate to the relevant circumstances and risks, including measures to prevent, detect, respond to, resolve and control for data poisoning, model poisoning, adversarial examples or model evasion, confidentiality attacks and model flaws.

Yes. A provider of a stand-alone high-risk AI system listed in Annex III must register itself and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service, under Article 49.1, which is the registration obligation Article 16.1(i) imposes on providers. The database itself is the EU database set up and maintained by the Commission under Article 71, with the provider or its authorised representative entering the Annex VIII Section A and B data. Two qualifications apply. Systems falling under Annex III point 2, critical infrastructure, are registered at national level instead under Article 49.5. Where the provider concludes under Article 6.3 that its Annex III system is not high-risk, it must still document that assessment under Article 6.4 and register itself and the system under Article 49.2.

High-risk. Biometric identification of travellers by or on behalf of competent public authorities in the context of migration, asylum or border control management is a listed use case under Annex III.7(d), which covers detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons and carves out only the verification of travel documents, so Article 6.2 classifies the system as high-risk. Mere document verification would fall outside that point, but biometric identification of the person does not. The provider must therefore meet the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and the full Article 16 provider set: a quality management system under Article 17, technical documentation under Article 11, retention of the automatically generated logs under Article 19, conformity assessment under Article 43, the EU declaration of conformity under Article 47 with the Annex V content, CE marking under Article 48, and registration under Article 49. Because the system falls under Annex III point 7, Article 49.4 requires that registration in the EU database established by Article 71 be made in the secure non-public section, accessible only to the Commission and the national authorities referred to in Article 74, with the restricted Annex VIII and Annex IX information. A provider established outside the Union must also appoint an authorised representative by written mandate under Article 22 before the system is placed on the market.

A fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27(1), which the public authority must perform prior to first deployment because it is a body governed by public law deploying a high-risk system under Article 6(2), namely the Annex III.5(a) use case of evaluating eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services and granting, reducing, revoking or reclaiming them. The assessment must set out a description of the deployer's processes in which the system will be used in line with its intended purpose, the period of time and frequency of intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to those categories taking account of the information given by the provider under Article 13, a description of the implementation of human oversight measures according to the instructions for use, and the measures to be taken if those risks materialise, including internal governance arrangements and complaint mechanisms. The duty attaches to first use, and previously conducted assessments may be relied on in similar cases, with updates required where any element changes under Article 27(2). Separately, before putting the system into service the authority must register itself, select the system and register its use in the EU database established by Article 71, as required by Article 49(3).

The media company, as deployer of the AI system generating or manipulating the video, must disclose under Article 50.4 that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. That deepfake disclosure duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Where the video forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, disclosure is limited to revealing the existence of the generated or manipulated content in a manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. Human review or editorial responsibility does not excuse a deepfake; that carve-out applies only to the separate Article 50.4 duty on AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. The provider of the generating system must separately mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated under Article 50.2, and under Article 50.5 the disclosure must reach the natural persons concerned in a clear and distinguishable manner at the latest at the time of first exposure.
